sessions.title: End to End Software Development Lifecycle Hardening with AMPEL
sessions.abstract:
As software delivery accelerates, teams need automated ways to verify compliance and security controls across the SDLC.

Hardening a pipeline means checking many things: who can run CI, whether repositories are configured safely, cryptographically verifying commit authors, whether tools and build chains have trusted provenance, auditing for vulnerabilities, and if all this is acceptable before release.

Yes there's a tool for each step, but stitching them together quickly becomes an unmaintainable mess.

Enter AMPEL, the supply chain policy engine. AMPEL uses policy as code to evaluate each stage of the SDLC, blocking builds when conditions are not met. Uniform, reusable policies help protect your systems, users, and organization from insecure releases.

In this hands-on session, we’ll use community-driven policies to lock down steps, monitor checks, and map controls to frameworks like the OSPS Baseline and NIST SSDF. Bring a project and a laptop; let’s harden it together.

Flux began in 2016 as the first tools to put Git at the center of Kubernetes delivery, and "GitOps" grew up alongside it.

After a brief look back, this talk focuses on where Flux is going. We'll cover the features shipped this past year across the GitOps Toolkit and Flux Operator, then dig into two shifts that define the next decade. First is wiring Flux into AI agents and the second is bringing Flux closer to developers through the Flux Operator UI.

The session concludes with the Flux roadmap and opportunities for community contribution.

sessions.title: Handing a Proxy the Keys to Your Pod: Inside Cilium's Sidecarless mTLS
sessions.abstract:
Cilium 1.19 shipped sidecarless mTLS reusing ztunnel, a proxy from Istio's ambient mode: label a namespace, and traffic between its pods is encrypted and identity-authenticated over HBONE, with no app changes necessary. But underneath that one line is a per-node proxy opening sockets inside pods it was never installed into, and a control plane fanning that label out to every node.

So how does it actually work? We'll walk from that label to the kernel primitives beneath it: the file-descriptor hand-off that opens listeners inside your pod, the StateDB reconciler that turns a namespace label into per-node state, how its SPIFFE identity is issued, and the in-pod iptables redirect that intercepts traffic.

You'll leave knowing how the pieces fit and where its edges are today (beta, TCP-only). We close on the SPIRE work we're upstreaming, which binds a certificate to the requesting process, not just to a pod, with a live demo: steal a cert without attestation, then watch SPIRE refuse.

sessions.title: How Ericsson Combines Human Judgment to Enhance AI-Powered Capabilities Through Backstage
sessions.abstract:
AI capabilities accelerate individual tasks but leave the SDLC static — bottlenecks simply migrate between stages. This session presents an AI-native architecture where specialized agents operate at every lifecycle stage while an AI Monitor provides system-level governance.

From Developer Experience (DX) at Ericsson, we show how these patterns extend across the SDLC, integrated into our Backstage-powered IDP.

The AI Monitor correlates upstream causes with downstream failures, surfacing improvements to human engineers who evaluate and implement changes. Humans remain in the loop as decision-makers bringing domain context agents cannot infer alone.

With Backstage as our single source of fresh, human-verified truth, we built AI capabilities on deterministic-first principles — using selective LLM escalation to minimize cost while maximizing reliability — integrated into our IDP.

Learn to pair system-level intelligence with human expertise to build self-improving golden paths.

sessions.title: Rolling Out LLM Inference Engines on Kubernetes: Capacity, Topology, and Deployment Verification
sessions.abstract:
Updating an LLM inference engine is not the same as rolling a stateless Kubernetes service. Each engine deployment carries GPU shape, topology, memory layout, prefill/decode balance, and startup cost. At OpenAI, a deployment preflight pipeline can keep GPU-backed pods pinned for hours during startup, warmup, and validation, creating capacity, scheduling, topology, and rollout challenges for the Kubernetes fleet.

Using the deployment preflight pipeline as a case study, the talk explains how quota, GPU topology, model architecture, cluster readiness, and availability targets become rollout admission checks, and how operators reason about compatible capacity, topology fit, rollback conditions, and blocked updates. Attendees will leave with portable patterns for deploying LLM engines when capacity and topology matter as much as pod readiness.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 254

speakers.name: Meng Dong
speakers.title: Member of Technical Staff
speakers.bio: Meng Dong works on applied scheduling and fleet orchestration for large-scale AI inference at OpenAI, focusing on GPU capacity, topology-aware placement, rollout safety, and Kubernetes-based production operations. Her work connects platform scheduling, cluster readiness, and deployment workflows to help inference services deploy reliably under tight capacity constraints.

speakers.name: Zihan Zheng
speakers.title: Member of Technical Staff
speakers.bio: Zihan Zheng is a Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI, where he works on large-scale inference systems for frontier models. His research focuses on AI evaluation, coding agents, and benchmark design. He led LiveCodeBench Pro and has authored work published at NeurIPS, ICLR, and ICML. He received his B.S. in Computer Science from NYU.

sessions.title: Who Keeps It Open?
sessions.abstract:
Every generational shift in computing produces plumbing that everyone depends on. TCP/IP, HTTP, the container runtime. And every time, there is a window where someone can quietly come to own it, and everyone else pays rent. The plumbing for AI agents is in that window right now.

This talk is about why it matters. Why “open” is a present-tense word, decided one release at a time unless neutral governance makes it permanent. Why the agentic layer captures something bigger than social media ever did, why a protocol owned by one vendor is just private property and you can get kicked out.

And why the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) is that neutral home for the agentic stack, which will guarantee openness, transparency, and access, and why over 300 companies have joined the AAIF to help further this mission.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom ACE

speakers.name: Manik Surtani
speakers.title: CTO and Co-founder
speakers.bio:
Manik is co-founder and CTO of the AAIF, ensuring AI agents are built on open foundations. He launched AAIF while at Block (fka Square), bringing years of experience in open source and infrastructure to a new set of challenges.

He spent over a decade at Block, as a staff IC and eng leader, including VP of Eng for Platform at CashApp. Most recently, he led Open Source at Block.

An author, investor, advisor and former venture scout, he speaks about agentic AI, open source and eng leadership.

sessions.title: MCP Without Polling: Building Reactive Agents with Continuous Queries
sessions.abstract:
Polling current state forces agents to trade freshness for repeated queries and can miss conditions that appear and disappear between checks. Forwarding every raw change makes models spend expensive tokens deciding which events matter.

This session shows MCP developers and agent builders how continuous graph queries in Drasi turn changes in existing data sources into streams of meaningful business events. Examples include orders becoming high-value and orders remaining unprocessed beyond a deadline, even when no new database write occurs.

The demo follows an agent discovering streams, choosing a subscription, and using MCP tools to investigate and act when a relevant event arrives. A prototype of MCP's emerging Events extension, a proposed standard for event discovery and subscriptions, connects producers and agents.

Attendees will learn to separate event detection from agent reasoning, understand query-result transitions, and combine event subscriptions with authoritative tool calls.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom ACE

speakers.name: Aman Singh
speakers.title: Engineering Leader at Microsoft Azure CTO's Office · Drasi Maintainer · CNCF organizer

sessions.title: Is Platform Engineering and the Platform Maturity Model Still Relevant in the Agentic AI Era?
sessions.abstract:

With the landscape changing almost on a daily basis, where agentics such as OpenClaw and AWS Kiro are only 6-12 months old, consultancies and vendors preaching new operating models and practices, lots of MVP’s and POCs showing benefits but not many talking about Production, what’s the real life discussions and feedback in the Platform Engineering community?

Come listen to two Platform Engineering practitioners and leaders who have been working on minor updates to the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model and their perspectives.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom BDF

sessions.title: Beyond the Four Golden Signals: Observability for the AI Era
sessions.abstract: A system can return a 200, respond in milliseconds, and still be wrong. AI agents and LLMs challenge traditional notions of application health by introducing probabilistic outcomes and rapidly variable costs. The four golden signals remain essential, but they no longer tell the whole story. Let's explore why accuracy and cost should join the golden signals, giving teams a clearer view of whether AI-powered systems are not only running, but running well and delivering value.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 250 A-C

speakers.name: Stephen Hussey
speakers.title: Instana Group Product Manager
speakers.bio: Stephen Hussey is a Group Product Manager at IBM Instana, where he manages teams focussed on how AI is used inside observability to improve outcomes and efficiency, and also how observability applies to customers' AI-enhanced applications and services to ensure that customers can adopt AI with confidence.

sessions.title: An Agent Is Not a Function Call
sessions.abstract:
Most AI APIs are shaped like function calls: send input, receive output. Coding agents break that abstraction. They operate over time, keep state across turns, stream intermediate work, act on workspaces, consume budgets, and sometimes need to be steered or interrupted.

Drawing from the design of the public OpenAI Codex Python SDK, this lightning talk asks what the right interface to an agent runtime should expose. The answer is not just a cleaner wrapper around inference. It is a set of control-plane primitives: threads for persistent context, turns for units of work, streams for observability, sandbox policies for workspace access, and result objects that preserve status, errors, timing, usage, items, and final output.

The central claim is simple: once a model can act, the API boundary becomes a safety boundary, an observability boundary, and a product boundary at the same time. Treating agents as function calls hides the machinery operators need to trust them.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 254

speakers.name: Shaghayegh Moradirad

Her work sits at the boundary of developer tools, AI systems, and product engineering. Before OpenAI, she worked on observability and large-scale infrastructure-adjacent systems at LinkedIn and Two Sigma.

sessions.title: Cluster Mesh, Native Routing, and Multi-pool IPAM in IPv6-Only Network: What the Docs Don't Tell You
sessions.abstract:
Last year we shared how ESnet, the U.S. Department of Energy’s high-performance research network, runs Kubernetes on-prem in IPv6 only network using Cilium. This talk covers what came next: building cluster-mesh using native routing, BGP, and multi-pool IPAM entirely without IPv4.

We'll walk through our architecture: why native routing over tunnels, how Cilium's BGP control plane with multi-pool IPAM enables pod-to-pod connectivity within and across clusters, and how we secure inter-cluster traffic with host firewall.

This isn't a feature walkthrough - we'll focus on what broke. Undocumented IPv6 PodIPPool mask size limitations silently blocked pod scheduling. Host firewall policies locked us out of control plane access and triggered etcd quorum loss, cascading into cluster-wide failures. For each, we'll show diagnosis, recovery, and prevention.

Attendees leave with a concrete IPv6-only cluster-mesh architecture, a trip-wire checklist, and hard-won lessons from production setup.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom J
tracks: Use Cases: End User Story Describing the Use of Cilium + Hubble + Tetragon to Overcome Challenges

speakers.name: Luke Baker

sessions.title: Creating VEX Documents at Scale: A Look into One Supplier's Process
sessions.abstract:
What is a VEX? What goes into it? How should you determine that? When and how should you create one? Why do you need one? This session answers those questions and more through a case study into how a large software supplier, Microsoft, is preparing to automate the creation of VEX documents. Specifically, the CSAF VEX specification required fields and options will be covered, however OpenVEX will also be investigated.

VEX documents are now a vital necessity for secure usage and inclusion of Open Source Software. They are required to supply software in compliance with EU CRA, alongside SBOM. With AI accelerating the rate of discovery of security vulnerabilities, VEX documents will be more and more applicable, as software suppliers will have trouble keeping up and many vulnerabilities are not exploitable.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 255 BC

Lately he has been building Microsoft's VEX document creation and tooling process. He is active in the OpenSSF and is a steering committee member of the OpenSSF Scorecard project. Jeff is a long time FOSS enthusiast and enjoys cycling in his spare time.

sessions.title: Pets, Cattle, and Herds: Fleet-Scale Continuous Delivery the GitOps Way
sessions.abstract:
GitOps grew up around a few hand-crafted environments, assuming a handful of pet targets you name and tend by hand. But these days retailers run a cluster per store, SaaS vendors spin up clusters per customer, and enterprises accumulate them faster than they can name them. The targets became cattle, and once there are thousands, committing and reviewing a spec for each by hand stops making sense. State has to be generated by automation, not authored in Git.

Argo CD gives you parts of the toolkit: ApplicationSets allow you to template your fleet, and Progressive Syncs roll changes out in health-gated waves. But it hits limits at fleet scale: approvals and notifications fire per Application, not once per rollout, and there's no first-class way to promote, gate, or view the herd as one.

We'll walk through the techniques and patterns for operating at this scale, showing where native patterns hold, where they break, and what the ecosystem is building to close the gap.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | 151

speakers.name: Jesse Suen

Prior to founding Akuity, Jesse was a Principal Software Engineer and technical lead for the Argo team at Intuit, leading the design and architecture for Workflows, CD, and Rollouts. Jesse was a founding engineer at Applatix, building a platform to help enterprises run containerized workloads in the public cloud. Jesse received his B.A. in Computer Science & Cognitive Science from UC Berkeley.

sessions.title: Your Backstage Portal Just Became an AI App Store
sessions.abstract:
Agents, MCPs, and AI skills are proliferating — but how do developers actually find, evaluate, and securely adopt them? We built an AI Catalog inside Backstage that turns your developer portal into a one-stop shop for AI assets.

In this lightning talk, I'll walk through the user journey: browsing available agents and MCP servers, reading their capabilities and ownership metadata, and installing them — all without leaving Backstage. No hunting through GitHub READMEs, no Slack threads asking "which agent does X?"

We'll see a live demo of the prototype and cover the key design choices: how we modeled AI assets alongside existing software components, what "install" means in the context of an AI skill, and how Backstage's existing plugin and catalog model turns out to be a surprisingly good fit for this problem.

If you're thinking about how to make AI tooling discoverable and governable inside your organization, this talk is for you.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 255 EF

speakers.name: Evan Shortiss
speakers.title: Technical Marketing Manager
speakers.bio: Evan Shortiss is a Technical Marketing Manager at Red Hat. He helps customers and field teams succeed with cloud-native technologies, maintains demo and workshop infrastructure, and creates technical enablement content. He's focused on cloud-native technologies, building mobile and web applications, and services using JavaScript ecosystem technologies.

sessions.title: Zero-Touch App Team Onboarding: Powering Self-Service Kubernetes at Enterprise Scale with Flux
sessions.abstract:
At a large financial institution running Flux across hundreds of private and public cloud Kubernetes clusters, the question is how you make GitOps transparent to thousands of developers.
We'll share our fully automated, zero-touch GitOps onboarding platform targeting Flux-powered Kubernetes clusters — with no platform team intervention.
We'll review the architecture that makes this possible, covering how it meets production SLA requirements while preventing privilege escalation across team boundaries. You’ll see how we leverage the Flux Operator to simplify Flux lifecycle management, and we'll go over how we close the feedback loop for app developers by wiring Flux's notification-controller back into CI pipelines for observability into deployment status.
Whether you're building a platform for 10 teams or 10,000, this talk gives you a battle-tested blueprint for a self-service GitOps infrastructure engine that removes platform engineering team bottlenecks.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom H
tracks: Building Internal Developer Platforms with Flux

speakers.name: Tiffany Wang

speakers.bio: Tiffany Wang is Principal Engineer at Morgan Stanley, working in a platform engineering team that delivers regulatory enterprise compliant tooling and GitOps for multi-cloud Kubernetes at scale. She is a champion of GitOps and Flux with a decade of experience as an engineer in the healthcare, automotive, and cloud native industries, empowering developers to reduce time to deployment while improving reliability and reproducibility.

speakers.name: Anthony Burris

speakers.bio:

sessions.title: Agents Will Be Judged on Where They Run
sessions.abstract:
The agent ecosystem has grown up assuming a hosted frontier model and an outbound connection. That assumption is fine for a lot of use cases and disqualifying for a lot of others: regulated industries, public sector, anywhere data residency or air-gapped operation is the starting condition rather than an edge case.

Those constraints aren't going away, and the capability gap that made them painful is closing fast as open-weight models get good enough for scoped, tool-using work. This talk argues that placement is about to become a first-class design concern for agentic systems, not a deployment afterthought, and looks at what has to be true of the runtime for an agent loop to work with no egress: local tool access, local audit, local identity, and a lifecycle you can operate across sites you can't reach.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom ACE

speakers.name: Saad Malik
speakers.title: CTO & Co-Founder
speakers.bio: As the CTO and Co-founder at Spectro Cloud, Saad Malik leads technology strategy and innovation across modern infrastructure, Kubernetes, distributed systems, and enterprise AI. He is one of the core architects behind Spectro Cloud's PaletteAI platform and the Inference Launchpad, helping enterprises run and govern complex workloads across cloud, data center, edge, and regulated environments. Saad's expertise over the last two decades has helped enterprises with transformational products for enterprises, service providers, and consumers.

sessions.title: The Third Phase of Agent Autonomy: Agents That Know When to Act
sessions.abstract:
Agent autonomy has evolved in two phases so far. In the first, invoked agents (copilots, chatbots, CLIs) wait for a human to trigger them at the right moment, with the right prompt. In the second, background agents (cron jobs, rule-based automations) remove that friction but move the hard problem upstream: someone still has to predict when the agent should act and encode that logic in advance. Each works well in its own domain, but both break down when the situation is novel and fast-moving, and no one can predict what the agent will need to do

This keynote argues that agent autonomy is entering a third phase: agents that decide for themselves when to engage and when to stay quiet. The core question shifts from ""can the agent do the task?"" to ""can the agent tell when the task needs doing?"" That shift creates a new set of design problems for anyone building or operating agents on cloud native infrastructure.

We'll use live incident response as the case study as it stress-tests autonomy like few environments can: the failures are unpredictable, the stakes are high, and the agent has to judge on its own when and how to get involved. The lessons come from Traversal's experience running autonomous agents inside production incident channels at large enterprises.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 250 A-C

speakers.name: Jason Schechner
speakers.title: SRE Researcher & AI Adoption Engineer
speakers.bio: SRE with a career older than the term "SRE".  I've done it all, seen it all, and (hopefully) learned at least a few lessons along the way.  Life-long tinkerer, habitual puzzle-solver, SCUBA diver and enthusiast for anything interesting.

sessions.title: Kubernetes under Fire: Igniting Performance and Burning Through Bottlenecks with Kube-Burner
sessions.abstract:
What happens when your Kubernetes cluster is pushed to its limits—does it scale or break in unexpected ways?

In this lightning talk, I’ll show how kube-burner is used to stress-test clusters, uncover performance bottlenecks, and catch regressions early.

Through quick examples, you’ll see how to run benchmarks, capture meaningful metrics, and identify issues like resource startup latencies and control plane slowdowns.

We’ll also highlight its role in upstream efforts like Kubernetes SIG KubeVirt and SIG Scalability, along with the project’s current scope and upcoming areas of development.

If you care about scalability and performance, this session gives you a fast, practical starting point.
sessions.room: Hyatt Regency | Level 4 | Regency Ballroom B-D

speakers.name: Andrew Collins

speakers.bio: Andrew is a Principal Software Engineer at Red Hat, focused on scaling and monitoring Kubernetes-based platforms.

sessions.title: An Agent-Ready Checklist for the Argo Project
sessions.abstract: AI agents can write code faster than any team can review it. But, that speed only matters if production stays stable. This keynote looks at what Argo needs for its next phase of agentic delivery across three fronts: integration (hint: Argo MCP server), progressive delivery (spoilers: Argo Rollouts), and traceability (the biggest gap).
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | 151

sessions.title: Signals to System Intelligence: How Platform Teams Move from Observability to Intelligent Operations
sessions.abstract: Kubernetes generates endless signals, but signals alone don't solve problems. IBM Concert helps platform teams connect observability, risk, performance, and cost data into a unified operational view, enabling faster decisions and coordinated action across tools and teams. Learn how agentic operations can help reduce complexity, improve availability, and move from insight to action at scale.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom BDF

speakers.name: Murtuza Mukadam
speakers.title: Senior Product Manager
speakers.bio: Murtuza Mukadam is a Senior Product Manager at IBM Turbonomic, where he leads the strategy and roadmap for container platform optimization and automation. With over 12 years of experience spanning software development and DevOps leadership, he excels at translating complex engineering challenges into tangible business value. He brings expertise in Kubernetes, Red Hat OpenShift, and cloud‑native platforms and architectures, enabling organizations to build scalable, high-performance systems.

sessions.title: Context Is the New Code: How Spotify Runs Agentic Engineering at Scale
sessions.abstract: Spotify built Backstage to tame the complexity of thousands of engineers and services, and AI agents bring that same complexity back at a whole new scale. Portal is the control plane for agentic engineering: it gives every agent your organization’s context, lets leaders govern models, cost, and standards across any model or agent, and learns from every session so your agents improve with every run. Xirp, Spotify’s agentic suite, is where engineers run and manage those agent sessions, on their desktop, in the cloud, or from their phone.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 255 EF

sessions.title: MCP Is the New Internal API Surface
sessions.abstract:
MCP makes it radically easier to expose tools, data, and actions to agents. That’s great. It also means organizations are about to create a lot of MCP servers.

We’ve seen this pattern before with internal APIs: rapid adoption, duplicated capabilities, unclear ownership, inconsistent standards, stale interfaces, and eventually a platform team asking, “Wait, how many of these do we have?”

In five minutes, we’ll look at what the last decade of API and platform engineering can teach us about the next few years of MCP, and which mistakes we really don’t need to make twice.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom ACE

speakers.name: Baruch Sadogursky
speakers.title: Head of DevRel
speakers.bio:
Baruch Sadogursky (@jbaruch) did Java before it had generics, DevOps before there was Docker, and DevRel before it had a name. He built DevRel at JFrog from a ten-person company through an IPO, co-authored "Liquid Software" and "DevOps Tools for Java Developers," and is a Java Champion, a Microsoft MVP for AI, and a CNCF Ambassador alum.

Today he's head of DevRel at Port, working on the agentic SDLC, and a self-certified Level 3 AI Context Sommelier.

sessions.title: Portable by Design: Accelerator-Agnostic Inference on Kubernetes
sessions.abstract:
For most organizations, the inference stack was built around a single accelerator vendor, often by default rather than by design. That assumption is now a liability. Accelerator supply, pricing, and performance are shifting faster than infrastructure roadmaps. Teams whose serving stack is tied to one hardware ecosystem are paying for it in constrained capacity, limited negotiating leverage, and slower time to production.
In this keynote, Vultr draws on its experience running NVIDIA and AMD accelerators side by side in production. It argues that hardware portability should be a first-class design principle for cloud native AI. The session looks at where vendor coupling builds up in real-world inference platforms and how recent advances in Kubernetes and the open source serving ecosystem make portability achievable today. It also identifies the gaps the community still needs to close. Attendees will leave with a practical approach to building inference infrastructure that can follow capacity, cost, and performance wherever they lead.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 254

sessions.title: Release, Observe, Decide: OpenFeature Meets OpenTelemetry
sessions.abstract: Your tests pass. You enable a feature for a small group of users. What evidence justifies expanding the rollout? This five-minute keynote follows one illustrative change from feature flag to production feedback. OpenFeature provides a standard interface for evaluating flags. OpenTelemetry instrumentation connects flag evaluations with runtime behavior. Together, they help teams investigate which requests received a change and decide whether to expand exposure or disable the feature. The same discipline applies whether a human or an AI coding agent wrote the code. Attendees leave with a practical release habit: define the evidence for proceeding, limit initial exposure, and verify the outcome before taking the next step.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 250 A-C

speakers.name: Sean O'Dell
speakers.title: Head of Developer Experience
speakers.bio: Sean O’Dell focuses on all things Developer Experience at Dynatrace. A reformed infrastructure administrator and architect, Sean brings experience from Infra, Cloud, Dev and Ops, with a passion for helping developers thrive in today’s cloud-native and AI-native world. Outside of work, Sean enjoys spending time with his family, gaming, watching TV, cheering on Arsenal, Alabama football, the New York Yankees, and the Tennessee Titans—and smoking Texas BBQ.

sessions.title: Upstream First Security: Keeping Telco Infrastructure Secure at Cloud Native Scale
sessions.abstract:
Telco infrastructure runs on bare metal that powers 5G mobile networks. When a CVE drops in Go dependency used by the stack, we cannot wait until next quarter. Telco regulatory requirements mean patch latency is measured in days. Time from discovery to exploitation has shank from days to hours, we've had to rethink how we work with OS and adopt a strict upstream-first approach.
We maintain bare metal Kubernetes infrastructure by using CNCF projects such as Metal3 and Cluster API. This talk covers how we triage CVEs across a dependency tree spanning 15+ upstream repositories, why we always fix issues upstream first instead of local patches, and how we structure release cadence so that production stays within one minor version of the latest.
We will share numbers, including the time to fix CVEs and the cost of backporting vs. upgrading. We discuss how we automated dependency scanning in multi-repository CNCF project. This are mechanics of keeping infrastructure secure with open source.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 255 BC

speakers.name: Jan Melen
speakers.title: General Manager
speakers.bio:
Jan Melén is an expert in networking, open-source software, and cloud technologies, with a career spanning over two decades. He is a staunch advocate for Free and Open-Source Software (FOSS) adoption within Ericsson and the broader community he engages with.

Since 2019, Jan has led a team dedicated to CNCF open-source projects, contributing to Ericsson's K8s distribution, and fostering an "upstream-first" culture. He oversees Ericsson’s open-source contributions and collaboration with CNCF.

speakers.name: Kashif Khan
speakers.title: Co-Chair CNCF TAG Infrastructure, Maintainer, Open Source Architect
speakers.bio: Kashif Khan is a co-chair of CNCF TAG Infrastructure and maintainer of the CNCF project Metal3.io for 6 years. He works as an open source Architect for Ericsson Software Technology, Finland. He holds a PhD in Computer Science. Kashif is a research and open source enthusiast and his current area of interest is kubernetes deployments on baremetal systems in distributed cloud scenarios.

sessions.title: OpenChoreo: Developer Platform for Both Humans and Agents
sessions.abstract:
Kubernetes gives platform teams powerful building blocks. But turning those into a real developer experience takes months of work. OpenChoreo is a complete, open-source developer platform for Kubernetes. It's ready to use from day one, for both humans and agents.

In this lightning talk, I'll walk through how OpenChoreo provides development and platform abstractions on top of Kubernetes. It comes with a Backstage-powered developer portal, plus built-in CI/CD, GitOps, and observability. Developers can self-serve deployments without needing to be Kubernetes experts.

These same abstractions also work well for AI agents. Agents need to build, deploy, and operate workloads too, often alongside humans. I'll share what it means to design a platform that serves both audiences from the start.
sessions.room: Hyatt Regency | Level 4 | Regency Ballroom B-D

speakers.name: Sameera Jayasoma
speakers.title: VP & Distinguished Engineer
speakers.bio: Sameera Jayasoma is a Vice President and Distinguished Engineer at WSO2, where he leads the technical direction of OpenChoreo, a CNCF project, and serves as one of its core maintainers. Sameera is the lead architect of the Ballerina platform, a programming language optimized for cloud-native integration. He is a dedicated mentor and frequent conference speaker, passionate about advancing developer productivity through technical innovation.

sessions.title: From Scarcity to Self-Service: Rethinking GPU Access for Platform Teams
sessions.abstract:
As AI workloads move into production, GPUs have become the most contested resource on the internal platform. Platform teams supporting AI often face two conditions that seem to contradict each other: teams waiting weeks for accelerator access, and expensive accelerators sitting allocated but idle. These are not separate problems. Both are symptoms of access models designed around scarcity, which reward teams for holding capacity rather than releasing it.

In this keynote, Vultr argues that GPU scarcity inside an organization is often the result of platform design rather than limited supply, and that platform engineering is well placed to fix it. Drawing on experience supporting AI teams building on Kubernetes, the session explores how the principles that made compute, storage, and databases self-service can apply to accelerators without giving up governance or cost control. Platform leaders will leave with a clear framework for raising accelerator utilization, reducing time to GPU, and tying AI infrastructure spend to business value.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom BDF

speakers.name: Mirdul Swarup
speakers.title: Manaager, Developer Relations
speakers.bio: Mirdul Swarup is Manager, Developer Relations at Vultr, focused on empowering developers to build scalable, production-ready cloud and AI workloads. He specializes in GPUs, Kubernetes, distributed systems, and infrastructure automation, creating technical content, talks, and hands-on guides that simplify complex infrastructure for modern engineering teams.

sessions.title: You’re Overspending on a Misconfigured Argo CD: Let’s Fix It
sessions.abstract:
Argo CD is incredibly powerful and has tons of knobs and dials to configure behavior, performance, and policy. All that configuration isn’t always intuitive and in our experience we’ve found it’s very common for organizations to adopt anti-patterns and create traps for themselves. We’ve spent the last 6 years compiling the most common and potentially devastating issues and will show how you can easily detect and fix these issues before they cause an incident.

Beyond performance, stability, and developer productivity lies the frontier of costs! Most engineering teams are disconnected from their cloud spends and don’t have tracking inside Argo CD,  which makes it easy to overspend and miss opportunities for optimization. We’ll show you how you can give your Argo CD super powers to detect antipatterns, and track costs effectively.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | 151

speakers.name: Kelly McCarthy
speakers.title: Solutions Engineer
speakers.bio: Former HashiCorp Solutions Engineer now at Octopus Deploy, helping teams scale Continuous Delivery with tools like Terraform, Vault, Argo, and more. I’ve helped modernize pipelines across industries. Outside work, I’m running, cycling, or chasing Austin’s best BBQ and tacos.

sessions.title: Architecture Without Gatekeepers: Decoupling for Neutrality
sessions.abstract: Open source only works if the community can contribute without hitting a wall. We realized our architecture at OpenEverest was unintentionally biased toward specific tools, so we rebuilt it. I’ll share how we moved to a modular plugin system that decouples our core from specific operators. By supporting everything from Valkey to competing Postgres flavors, we’ve eliminated vendor lock-in and ensured the community—not the architecture—dictates the project's future.
sessions.room: Hyatt Regency | Level 4 | Regency Ballroom B-D

speakers.name: Marcin Gwozdz
speakers.title: Head of GTM
speakers.bio:
Proactive IT solutions professional advisor with combined business and technical knowledge: experienced in cross-sector enterprise software sales, building technical alliances, and supporting channel sales for years. Focused on open-source solutions, always ready to share knowledge.

My vision is that open source will be as sustainable in terms of product and revenue growth as proprietary solutions, as more and more entrepreneurs will work on open source projects.

sessions.title: Beyond GitOps: Extending Flux for the Enterprise  AI, Security, Air-Gapped Delivery and the Next Gen
sessions.abstract:
Flux has evolved from a GitOps toolkit into a foundation for secure, governed software delivery. But enterprise environments increasingly demand more: AI-assisted operations, richer platform automation, disconnected and air-gapped deployments, and stronger network security.

In this keynote, we look ahead at the evolution of Enterprise for Flux: an extensible platform built around the Flux Operator. We'll explore AI-powered GitOps, secure supply-chain artifact mirroring, schema-aware automation, and MCP-based operations, and show how these capabilities build on Flux primitives and avoid operational complexity.

Then we'll look beyond what exists today and ask the Flux community: what should come next?
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom H

speakers.name: Andrew Martin
speakers.title: CEO and Founder
speakers.bio: Andrew has an incisive security engineering ethos gained building and destroying high-traffic web applications. Proficient in systems development, testing, and operations, he is at his happiest profiling and securing every tier of a cloud native system, and has battle-hardened experience delivering containerised solutions to enterprise and government. He is CEO at https://control-plane.io

sessions.title: Path to Resilient App Delivery: AI Is Hard, Production Is Harder
sessions.abstract:
Moving from an AI prototype to a stable, production-grade application introduces complexities in scale, governance, and infrastructure management. Don’t get stuck between rapid innovation and operational instability!

In this session, we will map out the path to overcoming these hurdles. You will see what it means to build on a platform that is Frontier AI ready and demonstrate how to leverage it to provide resilient services to harness production grade delivery for AI Outcomes.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 254

speakers.name: Cheslav Versky
speakers.title: Principal Architect
speakers.bio: Cheslav Versky focuses on driving developer velocity by helping organizations build, scale, and optimize the adoption of CNCF-compliant Kubernetes and modern application architectures for large enterprises across the AMER region; he holds the title of Principal Architect.

sessions.title: Postcards From Tomorrow: Powering the Agentic Era Through Open Source
sessions.abstract: Cloud native excellence in open-weight model serving, training, and agent usage has arrived in Kubernetes, and cost is driving this imperative. Serving, retraining and refining, and using open weight models like Qwen from model registries like Hugging Face is now easy enough that the entire ecosystem is taking action, driving up density, precision, and performance. This year, every engineer -- and thanks to models, many who work in other roles -- can take advantage of a faster, more cost-effective, and more secure Kubernetes. Opportunities in cloud native AI are driving the entire industry and the community is meeting the moment, reducing dependence on frontier models for their workloads and creating a more independent future with open source. You’ll leave inspired to build your own custom learning loops to power your agents via open source software paired with open weight models.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom ACE

speakers.name: Ralph Squillace
speakers.title: Principal Product Manager
speakers.bio: Professionally trained in history; don't tell him, because he's professionally suffered in distributed applications for the past 20 years or so. A veteran of OSS wars inside the megacorp, he's thrived as the world changed. Ralph is Microsoft's representative on the board of the Bytecode Alliance Foundation and is responsible for WebAssembly and other virtualization projects, including model serving and post training and other AI related workloads in Kubernetes.

sessions.title: The Future of Observability Is Thousands of Open AI Agents Built by You
sessions.abstract: AI SRE should be built on open standards and accessible telemetry, so teams can choose their own models, tools, and workflows. Every production environment has its own incidents, runbooks, and operational knowledge. Agents need that context to investigate. Engineers should be able to inspect the evidence behind conclusions, see which tools were called, reuse investigations, and control production actions. This keynote makes the case for open AI SRE foundations built by teams who run production.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 250 A-C

speakers.name: Mike Shi
speakers.title: Head of Product, Observability
speakers.bio: Mike leads observability at ClickHouse, where he works on ClickStack, a developer-focused observability platform. He joined ClickHouse through the acquisition of HyperDX, a company he co-founded, after spending five years building tools for engineers and gradually becoming a database person along the way. Now, he focuses on improving open-source observability tooling, from polishing buttons and docs to optimizing search and ingestion infrastructure.

sessions.title: After Mythos: The CVE Firehose Meets Tetragon
sessions.abstract: Mythos made the vulnerability backlog feel less like a queue and more like a firehose - and we can’t patch fast enough to keep up. To bridge the gap we need protection at runtime, and thankfully eBPF enables it in a highly performant way. This talk will share the latest developments in using Tetragon to provide guardrails and mitigations that you can deploy without downtime.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom J

speakers.name: Liz Rice
speakers.title: Chief Open Source Officer
speakers.bio:
Liz Rice is Chief Open Source Officer with eBPF specialists Isovalent, acquired by Cisco in 2024, and the creators of the Cilium cloud native networking, security and observability project. The author of Container Security, and Learning eBPF, both published by O'Reilly, Liz is also an award-winning speaker known for demystifying complex technical topics through demos and live coding. She serves on the CNCF Governing Board, and was previously on the Board of OpenUK. She was Chair of the CNCF's Technical Oversight Committee in 2019-2022, and Co-Chair of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon in 2018.

She has a wealth of experience from working on network protocols, distributed systems, AI, and software security. Liz loves riding bikes in places with better weather than her native London, and making music under the pseudonym Insider Nine.

sessions.title: Making Environments Repeatable: From Tools to Platform Capabilities
sessions.abstract:
Platform teams often repeat the same work when delivering environments to developers: installing tools, connecting services, passing configuration and checking that everything is ready. As more teams need these environments, manual setup becomes harder to scale.
This keynote explores how reusable stacks bring together the setup steps, configuration and readiness checks behind a complete environment. We'll share the thinking behind this approach and how it helps platform teams make environments easier to deliver, maintain and offer through self-service.

Attendees will leave with practical questions to guide their own approach: what should be reusable, what proves an environment is ready, and what should the platform handle for its users?

sessions.title: Code Nobody Wrote: Running Agents You Can't Trust
sessions.abstract: An agent writes a script, runs it, and moves on. Nobody reviewed it, nobody approved it, and no author ever existed to vouch for it. In 2026 that agent is often running inside a pod on your cluster. To be useful it needs real credentials, and to be productive it runs with no human watching and approving each step. If you deploy agents, then allowing this safely is your responsibility, and how you do it depends on two things. What does the workload need? And who is driving it?
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom ACE

speakers.name: Todd Neal

speakers.bio: Todd is a Principal Software Engineer at AWS working on the Kubernetes data plane, with a current focus on the trust boundaries between workloads and the infrastructure they run on. His broader work covers the security, reliability, and robustness of Kubernetes nodes and the runtimes that host workloads on them.

sessions.title: Your Agents, Your Rules, Your Safety: Sovereign AI for the Agentic Era
sessions.abstract:
The rapid evolution of agentic capabilities has catapulted AI safety to the top of the agenda in boardrooms and governments alike. The enterprise threat model changes fundamentally as modern agents don't just generate text -- they execute code, manage credentials, and interact directly with live production systems. In this new paradigm, securing AI cannot rely solely on model guardrails and prompt-layer intent shaping; it demands a defence-in-depth strategy anchored at the infrastructure execution layer.

This session reframes Sovereign AI for the Agentic Era. Sovereignty is not just a data-residency checkbox or a cost-forecasting exercise -- it is the fundamental capability to own your intelligence rather than simply rent it. Drawing on open-source cloud-native building blocks, we will share how platform teams can safely adopt agents at scale without sacrificing portability, cost predictability, full-stack auditability, or runtime security.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 254

speakers.name: Abhinav Puri
speakers.title: VP & General Manager Portfolio & Community
speakers.bio: Abhinav Puri is Vice President and General Manager, Portfolio & Community at SUSE, where he leads portfolio management for SUSE's enterprise infrastructure portfolio across Cloud native, AI, Edge and Linux. A cloud native product leader by background, he led SUSE's entry into AI, launching the company's first AI solutions to help enterprises run AI on open, secure and sovereign infrastructure. He also oversees SUSE's engagement with the open source communities that underpin its portfolio.

sessions.title: Celebrate Flux's 10 Years!
sessions.abstract:
Flux turns 10!
This talk gives an overview of GitOps and Flux (the CNCF graduated project) and why Flux has been the most trusted tool for cloud providers, small to enterprise customers, and across financial institutions to telcos.
Flux continues to push boundaries in security, scalability, and reliability:
- Security-first design including SOPS with Age post-quantum cipher, Workload Identity, verification, CoSign, and the Flux UI with RBAC, SSO, and more
- Massive scale through design, data size, and network efficiency: Kubernetes server-side apply, horizontal and vertical pod autoscaling, artifact size reduction, and multiple artifact source and data types options
- Flux’s modularity: use only needed Flux controllers, no CPU bottlenecks from app bloat, and now a Flux CLI plugin system for added capabilities
- Flux’s use of the Helm SDK for full capabilities including supporting Helm’s post-render strategies, literal mode, and more
Celebrate Flux’s 10th anniversary with us at KubeCon!

sessions.title: OpenChoreo: Developer Platform for Humans & Agents
sessions.abstract:
AI agents are becoming active participants in software delivery, writing code, operating infrastructure, and automating platform workflows. Rather than building separate systems for AI, platform engineering must evolve the Internal Developer Platform itself.

In this keynote, we'll explore what it takes to build an Internal Developer Platform that enables both humans and AI agents to operate under the same guardrails, identities, and golden paths. Using OpenChoreo as a practical example, we'll show how a modern Kubernetes-first platform unifies portals, APIs, CLI, GitOps, and MCP with built-in platform agents, such as SRE and FinOps agents, that work alongside developers and platform engineers to improve reliability, operations, and cost optimization.

The future of platform engineering isn't human-only or agent-only, it's one platform where humans and AI agents collaborate securely.

sessions.title: Container Builds at Scale with Buildpacks
sessions.abstract:
Cloud Native Buildpacks transform your application source code into images that can run on any cloud. They enable advanced caching mechanisms that improve performance at scale. They also allow for modularity and reuse, which ensure developers across your organization aren’t wasting cycles repeating what other teams have already done.

After this short talk, you’ll be able to run buildpacks with the Pack CLI and find off-the-shelf buildpacks in the Buildpack Registry, including those from Google, Heroku, and Paketo. Finally, you’ll learn how operators of large platforms use buildpacks to make their container builds as scalable as possible.

sessions.title: Simplifying Distributed LLM Serving: What's New in KServe
sessions.abstract:
As generative AI reshapes how organizations build and deploy intelligent applications, the demands on model serving infrastructure keep rising, teams need distributed execution, efficient autoscaling, and multi-tenant isolation, all without adding operational complexity. This session explores how KServe, a CNCF incubating project, continues evolving to meet these challenges head-on.

We're excited to walk through latest releases of KServe. These releases introduce multi-node inference without requiring a Ray head node, LeaderWorkerSet-based autoscaling for distributed workloads, and an upgrade to llm-d v0.6 for disaggregated prefill/decode serving. It also adds OpenAI Responses API routing, namespace-scoped ModelCache for multi-tenant model caching, and all the latest vLLM features, alongside meaningful security hardening across the platform.

Join us to see how KServe is simplifying production-grade LLM serving, one release at a time.

His key interests are systems involving the next generation of AI workloads, mainly inference at scale of AI Factories

sessions.title: Beating the Final Boss: GitOps Promoter in Production
sessions.abstract:
Environment promotion is the final boss of GitOps, forcing teams to build hacky imperative glue scripts or abandon GitOps entirely. Argo’s Progressive Syncs and Sync Waves work for basic use cases but fail for more complex requirements.

Intuit built something completely different, something fully declarative: GitOps Promoter, an OSS project in Argoproj Labs.

GitOps Promoter moves changes through environments by continuously evaluating gates. Gates pass, and changes ship, like falling dominoes: no buggy CI scripts to debug, no imperative steps to coordinate.

Productionizing GitOps Promoter at Intuit involved shipping new features: web request gates for change management, an Argo UI extension, multi-Argo instance support, etc. We’ll cover these plus features that helped ship GitOps Promoter for other adopters such as Red Hat and Circle.

We’ll catch you up to the environment promotion state of the art and let you know what’s around the corner for Argo and the GitOps ecosystem.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | 151

speakers.name: Michael Crenshaw
speakers.title: Senior Staff Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Michael Crenshaw is a Staff Software Engineer on the Argo CD team at Intuit. He is the most active contributor to the Argo project, focusing on security and performance improvements in Argo CD. He helps maintain Intuit’s ~50 Argo CD instances and ~20k Argo CD applications.

speakers.name: Zach Aller
speakers.title: Staff Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Zach Aller is a software engineer at Intuit and a lead maintainer of Argo Rollouts. He has 15+ years of software development experience with a strong focus on SRE/Platform tooling. He has a strong background in Kubernetes and has managed large scale Kubernetes clusters for multiple organizations. He is is a strong proponent in GitOps style deployments which he has implemented at scale.

sessions.title: Demystifying an Argo Workflows Pod — And How We Stopped Needing an Init Container
sessions.abstract:
When Argo Workflows runs your workload, your container isn't alone in its pod. Argo wraps other containers and volumes around it to feed your code its inputs and carry the results back out, and most people never notice any of that is happening.

This talk opens up the pod. We'll look at what each piece does: how your parameters and artifacts get in before your code starts, how the outputs and logs get back out after it finishes, and the little shared filesystem Argo uses to pass it all between containers. You'll come away actually knowing what Argo does for you every time a step runs.

Then we'll get to what's changed. Every Argo pod used to begin with an init container that staged things before your work started. Kubernetes now supports image volumes, which means we can drop that init container entirely. I'll show how this new opt-in feature in Argo Workflows 4.1 works, what you get for it, and the small things worth knowing before you switch it on.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 251 A-C

speakers.name: Alan Clucas
speakers.title: Staff Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Alan Clucas is an Staff Software Engineer at Pipekit, and project lead on Argo Workflows. His background is in software development and devops, and from this has come a love of open source. In his spare time he works on Crumbhole, a collection of Open Source GitOps tools using the Argo Project as a foundation.

speakers.name: Jason Meridth
speakers.title: Staff Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Jason Meridth (@jmeridth) is a Staff+ Software Engineer with over two decades of experience designing, building, and scaling software systems that power modern engineering organizations. My work spans cloud-native infrastructure, distributed systems, application development, and container orchestration, with a consistent focus on reliability, security, and developer experience.

sessions.title: Designing an Internal SLO Platform
sessions.abstract:
Most orgs have SLOs but don't trust them, because platforms are built around services — producing thousands of numbers nobody aggregates. Nubank built its SLO platform around business domains/subdomains instead, so questions like "are card payments healthy?" get one answer.

The talk covers: (1) why domains beat services as the unit; (2) the architecture — a dedicated VictoriaMetrics stack (vicmetrics-*-slo) isolated from main observability, running in six countries, with a Go API for registration and an slo-generator computing SLI/SLO from PromQL; (3) production lessons from running it across thousands of services — what worked, what didn't, what they'd redo.

Takeaway: a practical template for building SLOs on infra you already have (VictoriaMetrics/Prometheus, Grafana, small Go service) and a framework for what to prioritize.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 250 A-C
tracks: End User Stories: Production Deployments + Migrations + Operations

speakers.name: Julio Leal
speakers.title: Lead Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Júlio César Leal is a Site Reliability Engineer at Nubank with 20+ years in tech. He maintains observability infrastructure at massive scale — 1B+ time series, 50TB of metrics, and 6K alerts/min. Previously SRE at Softplan and SysAdmin at Unifor. Skilled in Kubernetes, Docker, Prometheus, Terraform, Ansible, Python, Golang, AWS and Azure. BSc in Computer Science, postgrad in Information Security.

sessions.title: Don’t Lose Your Agent’s Mind: Platform Patterns for Stateful Agents
sessions.abstract:
Agents accumulate context and session history over hours or days, but all of it can vanish in an instant. We deployed multiple agent harnesses like Claude Code and Hermes on Kubernetes and found they all break in similar ways: unrecoverable sessions and silent state loss. Existing harnesses assume stable filesystems and process continuity - assumptions Kubernetes violates. This infrastructure mismatch is a problem no individual harness will fix.

This talk presents platform patterns for managing agent state. We cover where existing primitives stop and what agents actually need from platforms, like durable sessions that survive node failure and state that follows the workload from local development to cloud. We demonstrate crash recovery progressing from “everything is lost” to transparent session resume and outline the future of state governance. Participants will leave with an adoptable Kubernetes-native reference architecture to support state-rich agentic workloads.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom BDF
tracks: Building Platforms for Day 2 and Beyond

speakers.name: Evaline Ju
speakers.title: Senior Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Evaline is a senior engineer working on the AI platform engineering team of IBM Research and based in Denver, Colorado. Her work focuses on platform-level concerns for agent workloads including guardrails and observability. She is also a contributor to the Kubernetes agentic networking group.

speakers.name: Maia Iyer
speakers.title: Advisory Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Maia is an Advisory Software Engineer at IBM Research specializing in platform engineering and cloud-native security. While deeply experienced in zero trust - a dedicated maintainer of SPIFFE's Tornjak project - her research now tackles the infrastructure demands of the AI era. An active and passionate speaker and writer, Maia now explores the intersection of agentic workloads and Kubernetes, and how cloud-native platforms must evolve to make AI agents run reliably and securely.

sessions.title: Don’t Make a Mesh of It: Multi-cluster Networking at Cloud Scale
sessions.abstract: Multi-cluster networking is moving from demos to production on public clouds, and the MCS-API is making the same shift to real workloads. At cloud scale this surfaces hard problems such as meshes spanning many large clusters, mixed network topologies, and operators who need precise control over what crosses a cluster boundary. Using Cilium Cluster Mesh as a case study, this talk examines two layers that make it practical. For sharing, service export is opt-in and scoped: per service through ServiceExport, or per namespace, so cross-cluster exposure is exactly what platform teams choose rather than on by default. For the data path, it shows how to align routing with topology, using native routing to avoid encapsulation on flat cloud networks instead of tunneling everything, so large meshes don’t pay VXLAN or Geneve overhead they don’t need. You’ll leave able to reason about the export model and the routing and scaling tradeoffs behind production multi-cluster networking.

sessions.title: From Geological Layers to NFS: Migrating a Decade of Backstage with AI
sessions.abstract:
Spotify's internal Backstage goes back to 2014, four years before Backstage even had a name. Over a decade it accumulated ancient plugins, stalled earlier migrations that left everyone stuck between old and new, and frontend sediment from every era of the company. An earlier attempt to modernize ran out of steam and nobody wanted to try again.

We tried again anyway, this time with AI doing most of the grunt work. About 150 plugins moved to the New Frontend System in roughly ten weeks, around half a million lines changed. Without AI agents handling the codemod volume, this migration would have stalled the same way the last one did.

The talk gets into the mechanics: how we iterated agent skills against a codebase few fully understood, swapped centralised app wiring for extension blueprints, used feature flags so teams could fall back to the old experience, and built a custom plugin to make migration progress visible to everyone.

sessions.title: From Helmfile to Flux: GitOps for Telco at Enterprise Scale
sessions.abstract:
Telco BSS/OSS software is mission-critical, heavily regulated, and notoriously hard to deploy. For a large product organization, rebuilding years of mature CI/CD pipelines just to “do GitOps” is non-starter. So how do you move an entire BOS portfolio to GitOps with Flux — without throwing away what already works, and without forcing every customer to change overnight?
This is our journey. We made continuous testing the foundation, then built a “helm2flux” conversion that automatically generates Flux manifests from existing Helm assets — no pipeline rebuilds, and room for customers to adopt continuous deployment at their own pace. Today we run microservices delivery and full Git-driven day-2/N configuration across the portfolio. Next: AIOps, using OpenTelemetry, MCP, and agent skills to let AI safely assist the lifecycle, with the security guarantees telco demands.
Jesus covers the org side; Carl-Fredrik covers tech. Expect honest lessons, reusable patterns, and a few scars.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom H
tracks: Running Flux at Scale in Production

sessions.title: From Routing Weights to Tail Latency: Simulating Kubernetes-Native LLM Inference Without GPUs
sessions.abstract:
How does a single routing weight change impact a 16-instance Kubernetes LLM cluster? It triggers a cascade through prefill/decode disaggregation, KV-cache eviction, and autoscaler loops, causing erratic tail latency spikes. Teams are forced to burn massive GPU budgets on test clusters just to safely tune a single production scheduling parameter.

Discrete-event simulation offers a systematic escape from this hardware bottleneck. By translating pipelines, KV-cache states, and routing logic into deterministic events, performance can be evaluated instantly. Validated across 50 configurations with a 10% median latency error, this approach mimics live hardware without a single GPU.

We break down how to map complex Kubernetes orchestration dynamics into lightning-fast execution events. Attendees leave with an understanding of how to leverage a high-fidelity, open-source simulation framework to accelerate critical workloads like complex policy exploration and automated capacity planning.

sessions.title: OpenTelemetry Far and Wide
sessions.abstract:
OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation made broad observability effortless: one command, zero code changes, every service covered. But breadth isn't always the whole story. OpenTelemetry SDK instrumentations operate at the language level, surfacing transaction details that can be lifesavers in debugging scenarios and provide invaluable insights to developers. The catch: rolling out SDK instrumentation across a diverse, multi-technology/multi-team ecosystem can be slow and expensive.

This talk introduces a practical approach that eliminates the tradeoff: by combining eBPF instrumentation with SDK auto-injection, teams get broad coverage immediately and deep, language-level insights where needed, with a single deployment mechanism and dynamic cost controls.

We’ll do a live demo of this combined instrumentation approach and show how with a single command we can instrument everything in our system, upgrade to new OpenTelemetry SDK versions and control the cost of our instrumentation.

sessions.title: Securing the Agentic Tool Layer: A Runtime Defense Framework for MCP Agent Deployments
sessions.abstract:
Most LLM safety work guards the user prompt. MCP agents face a different problem: the attack arrives through the tools the agent already trusts. A poisoned tool description, a hidden instruction in a tool response, or a malicious server pulled from a public registry can hijack an agent without ever touching the user.

This session walks through a threat taxonomy built from 80+ techniques catalogued under SAFE-MCP, a Linux Foundation/OpenSSF project, then shows a runtime proxy that validates tool calls and responses inline, with no changes to the agent or server. In red-team testing across five model backends, it cut tool-poisoning success from 74% to under 9% and indirect injection from 47% to under 6%, adding under 120ms per call.

Attendees leave with a concrete defense architecture, the false-positive tradeoffs that matter in production, and what to vet before approving an MCP server for their stack.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom ACE

sessions.title: The RCA Bot Needed an RCA: Compute Confidence, Don't Generate It
sessions.abstract:
Every postmortem now ends with the same footnote: automate the RCA. Our agents got faster at investigations but worse at answers, and each root cause came with a confidence the model wrote about itself.

This talk shows how an inference platform on Kubernetes can compute confidence instead. One request scores every candidate cause from token probabilities, calibration corrects overconfidence, and conformal prediction returns a short list that holds the true cause at a chosen rate. Confident, systematic misses survive calibration, so each suspect is checked in a forked Firecracker microVM on Agent Sandbox, running in under a second instead of a 10 second boot.

Then we serve the traffic this creates with NVIDIA Dynamo: cache-first routing for 12x faster follow-ups, a CPU cache tier the router can see, and severity as request priority. Every number is reproducible with open source code.

sessions.title: Why Post-quantum Authentication Will Break K8s (and How Merkle Trees Fix It)
sessions.abstract:
The industry is actively working to secure our key exchanges against quantum threats, but what about our identities? As industry leaders update their PQC migration timeline to 2029, the focus is urgently shifting from encryption to the untackled authentication challenge.
Traditional PKIs retrofitted with ML-DSA face crippling performance degradation from massive signatures and compute overhead. So, how do we secure K8s’ internal communication without grinding the control plane to a halt?
In this talk we:
+ detail the reality of (lacking) ML-DSA support across the ecosystem which makes even experimenting with PQC incredibly difficult
+ analyze the critical compute and size bottlenecks introduced by standard ML-DSA signatures with a local PKI and hard numbers
+ explore Merkle Tree Certificates as a high-performance alternative to side-step PQC signature limits
+ demonstrate how to run an MTC PKI locally and map out how K8s can adopt this approach for its internal certificate requirements

sessions.title: Extending the Immutable OS: Adding Tools to Flatcar with Systemd-Sysext
sessions.abstract:
Immutable operating systems make Kubernetes nodes much more predictable, but they also introduce a problem for new users: a read-only root filesystem. When you need to install debugging tools, eBPF tracers, or custom storage drivers, the usual habit of running a package manager just does not work.

This 5-minute talk shows a practical way to solve this using system extensions (systemd-sysext) in Flatcar Container Linux. I will explain how system extensions let platform teams dynamically overlay binaries onto a read-only OS at runtime. This keeps the atomic update model intact and respects the rules of immutability. You will walk away knowing how to keep your host OS strictly versioned while still having the flexibility to handle day-to-day debugging and hardware enablement.

sessions.title: Agentic GitOps: Agent and Sandbox Guardrails with Flux
sessions.abstract:
With agentic workflows, kubectl commands can have dangerous consequences. Improper RBAC can allow agents to kubectl delete, and that includes deleting your whole CI with no commits to roll back to!
That’s why Flux's security-first design is even more relevant for agentic GitOps. We'll cover how to use Flux to confine agents to human-reviewable PRs for all sorts of use cases. We’ll do this with a kernel-sandboxing tool called `nono`. In addition, for your agent management tool of choice, we'll cover how to manage your agents' sandboxes with Flux so that nefarious (or confused) agents can't destabilize the security policies that you have in place.
We’ll cover safe practices for agentic use cases like:
- using Prometheus metrics to trigger resource tuning
- troubleshooting and rolling back after HPA crashes
- agents requesting additional network access with PR’s for human reviewers

Come join in!

sessions.title: Building Governance for Hybrid Architectures for Agentic Systems
sessions.abstract:
Autonomous AI agents are shifting to dynamic orchestrators that switch between local open-source models and external closed LLMs. When an agent autonomously escalates complex requests to public APIs or falls back to a local model, managing data sovereignty, routing rules, and governance becomes a critical platform engineering hurdle.

This presentation offers an end-to-end traffic governance framework for hybrid agentic loops using CNCF infrastructure. We showcase a declarative architecture using Kuadrant to build a secure AI routing tier. By coupling SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identities with Kuadrant's authorization layer, we ensure external API keys are never exposed and only validated agents can invoke specific model endpoints managed by Kubeflow's KServe. Finally, we demonstrate how guardrails play an important role in governance, ensuring payload verification across both local and cloud-hosted model targets.

sessions.title: Cache Me If You Can: Optimizing Expensive Tasks in Argo DAGs
sessions.abstract:
AI and data workflows often run as DAGs in Argo Workflows. Related runs can repeat expensive steps such as OCR, embedding generation, document parsing, and model inference. Yet cache eviction is often based only on recency, which can discard an expensive result while retaining a cheaper one.

This session presents a Kubernetes-native caching proxy for Argo Workflows. The proxy runs alongside workflow tasks and uses task metadata to prioritize cached results by re-computation cost, DAG dependency count, and invocation frequency.  Attendees will see the proposed architecture, cache metadata, eviction flow, and an Argo deployment pattern for sharing reusable task results across related workflow runs. The approach is based on independent research that reported up to 51% lower latency than LRU in multi-agent benchmarks. The session translates that idea into a practical pattern for Argo users building AI and data pipelines on Kubernetes.

sessions.title: Endpoint Observability with OpenTelemetry Collector at Cisco IT
sessions.abstract: Employee laptops are production systems for IT, but most observability patterns still assume servers, clusters, or services. This session shares how Cisco IT used a custom OpenTelemetry Collector build to observe macOS, Windows, and Linux endpoints without turning every laptop into a high-cardinality telemetry source. The talk walks through the collector architecture: hostmetrics for CPU, disk, memory , and selected processes; httpcheck, tcpcheck, icmpcheck, and a custom pathcheck receiver for SaaS, Webex, DNS, proxy, VPN, and route diagnostics; and a loadlevel processor that keeps detailed process metrics only when CPU or memory pressure makes them useful. Attendees will see the trade-offs behind collection intervals, MTS reduction, route snapshots as logs instead of metric dimensions, privacy controls, and safe rollout profiles for large employee fleets.

sessions.title: Hardening Federal Open-Source CI/CD, One Pipeline at a Time
sessions.abstract:
US federal agencies (cisagov, GSA, NIST, and 300+ other orgs) publish open-source code on GitHub, but their CI/CD pipelines carry the same vulnerability patterns as everyone else: unpinned actions, overly broad tokens, and pwn-request triggers. Executive Order 14028 and the CISA SSDF set the mandate, but the gap between policy and workflow-level implementation is wide.

This talk covers what I found auditing federal repositories for CI/CD weaknesses, and the process of turning findings into accepted contributions. I share before-and-after examples, explain why least-privilege permissions matter even for public repos, and discuss practical challenges: review timelines, CLA processes, and framing a PR so it gets merged.

Over 320 merged security contributions across 75 organizations, with accepted fixes in NASA, NIST, and other federal agencies, plus private vulnerability disclosures to government repositories.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 255 BC

sessions.title: Kueue, DRA, and WAS: The Kubernetes Scheduling Triangle
sessions.abstract:
Modern AI workloads expose two gaps in Kubernetes scheduling. First, accelerators are no longer simple device counts: a MIG 1g.10gb slice and a 7g.80gb partition may count as “1 GPU” despite using vastly different capacity. Second, AI jobs need gang scheduling and topology-aware placement. kube-scheduler addresses these through Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) for accelerator modeling and Workload-Aware Scheduling (WAS) for workload-level placement. But clusters need quota and queuing, which Kueue provides.

We present Kueue’s integration with DRA, using Partitionable Devices to charge quota in units like GPU memory, not device count. MIG profiles sharing one quota pool can be charged by actual use.

Finally, we introduce scheduler-library, exposing kube-scheduler logic as compile-time building blocks for orchestrators like Kueue and Cluster Autoscaler. For Kueue, it combines scheduler-native accuracy with fast scheduling and preemption simulations for multi-tenant quota management.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 2 | 254

sessions.title: llm-d Observability: Observing LLM Inference at Scale on Kubernetes
sessions.abstract:
Production LLM inference on Kubernetes is distributed by design: requests flow through gateways, llm-d Router (EPP), KV-cache indexers, vLLM workers, and Prefill/Decode sidecars. Traditional metrics miss token-level latency, cache locality, and routing decisions, and that gap quietly erodes the 3x throughput gains from cache-aware scheduling.
This talk shares llm-d's (CNCF Sandbox) Observability: a component-level audit of metrics, traces, logs, dashboards, and alerts across the stack. We show what is already working (EPP and vLLM OTel, Prometheus scrapers, inference-sim for GPU-free CI) and the critical gap: cross-component trace linkage, zero pre-built dashboards, and opaque P/D KV transfers.
Attendees will leave with practical patterns: W3C TraceContext propagation, OTel Collector configs, tiered KV-cache observability, WVA autoscaling visibility, and a prioritized community roadmap for future release. Applicable beyond llm-d to any Kubernetes-native GenAI serving platform.

sessions.title: Platform Engineering's Missing Chapter: Services Organizations
sessions.abstract:
The consultant who just delivered a Kubernetes migration moves to the next engagement and rebuilds everything from scratch. So did three other teams last quarter.
Platform engineering was supposed to fix this. For product companies, it has. Golden paths, dedicated platform teams, internal developer platforms - the model works when your stack is stable & your developers are internal.
Service organisations never had that luxury. Consultancies, systems integrators, and delivery orgs operate where product playbooks break: different cloud per client, different CI/CD per engagement, different compliance posture every quarter.
This session introduces Delivery Capital - organisational knowledge that a services org accumulates across engagements - and the Capability Layer that makes it reusable.
We examine five pillars - cloud, IaC, CI/CD, observability, and monitoring - and show how each changes when the customer is external, the environment is unknown, and expertise must transfer fast
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom BDF

sessions.title: Running Out of IPs Before You Run Out of GPUs: IPv6 for AI-Scale Kubernetes
sessions.abstract:
You've provisioned the GPU nodes and sized the power, cooling, and storage. But have you planned the IP addresses? In a dense AI cluster, with dozens of pods per GPU node across a large fleet, a private range that looked endless on the whiteboard runs dry fast.

It usually isn't public IPv4 scarcity that forces the move. It's the quiet exhaustion of RFC1918 space inside the flat, multi-account networks AI platforms grow into. Add autoscaling and constant rebuilds, and your address plan becomes what caps your scale.

So is IPv6 the answer, and is it worth the cost? This talk argues that
for AI-scale Kubernetes, IPv6 is the substrate that makes the
architecture work. We'll look at teams running it in production, stay
honest about the sharp edges: IPv6 IP pools advertised over BGP, plus
the capacity math to size it yourself.
sessions.room: Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom J

sessions.title: Scaling OpenTelemetry in a Financial Enterprise: Lessons from CapitalOne's Journey
sessions.abstract:
Capital One has spent the past five years evolving OpenTelemetry from an early proof of concept into a vendor-agnostic, production-grade observability platform running across one of the largest cloud-native environments in financial services. Because Capital One operates as a fully regulated financial institution, that evolution also meant building compliance and audit requirements directly into the platform.
This talk covers the architectural redesigns driven by cost and value tradeoffs, and the agent extensions built to close gaps with commercial tooling. It also covers how Capital One rolled OpenTelemetry out across 85,000+ compute instances, 100,000+ Lambda invocations, and thousands of Fargate and Kubernetes workloads, without disrupting the experience application teams already relied on.
Attendees leave with lessons on phasing a large-scale rollout, building regulatory guardrails into an observability platform, and driving adoption across hundreds of application teams.
